There is now one puncture in each disk, and the intersection circle has not changed. In a disk a nonempty finite family of type-II chords cuts off at least two outermost disks; at least one of those contains no puncture. Choose an innermost empty subdisk if further intersection arcs lie in it and apply III. Repeating removes all type-II arcs, without changing $P$ or either puncture. Circles have already been removed. Each remaining puncture is on exactly one spanning disk on its own side, and a type-I arc has just one puncture endpoint. There are therefore exactly two type-I arcs in total. Their other endpoints are on $P\cap S$, away from $K$, and can be taken distinct by a small foot perturbation on $S$. Thus their union consists of two disjoint embedded arcs, as asserted. conserved_row.complete_before_row: 1.3 For an essential separating product annulus with connected R+ and R−, form the two rounded horizontal surfaces from opposite boundary faces and the annulus. Their actual cobordism regions give the required relative class and their Euler sums give the horizontal equality. This reduces the operation to attachment of a product region. A rooted cut-arc forest removes a product region meeting the sutures by literal product-disk identifications. For an interior essential product region, the explicit once-punctured-torus block forces its two fixed coordinates and isolates the only possible extra genus-one two-corner domain, whose Maslov index is minus one; it cannot contribute. Both comparison diagrams therefore have precisely the same supported disks and conjugate oriented operators in the unchanged complement. The resulting integral chain identification, followed by the remaining product-disk cuts, gives the full separating-annulus graded tensor operation. It gives Ni's field formula and the integral Künneth/Tor formulation as above. All constructions keep the stated basepoint zero regions, actual periodic lattices and essential-annulus hypotheses. They apply when the specified characteristic product region supplies those actual surfaces; they do not infer its geometry from generic disk existence. [F2, step 1.2] ∎

conserved_row.complete_before_row: 5.1 Write $p_n=p_{\alpha_n,0}$. Maximality against $p_0\in P_0$ and the support bound $\langle f,p_n\rangle_Y\le R(u^\dagger)$ give $\|p_n\|_Y\le\|p_0\|_Y$ and $\langle f,p_n\rangle_Y\to R(u^\dagger)$. The closed span of any subsequence is separable; Gram–Schmidt on rational finite linear combinations of its terms gives a finite or countable orthonormal family with dense span. Repeated use of [F8] and [A1] selects a further subsequence whose coordinates all converge. For each finite initial segment, expanding the nonnegative squared norm after orthogonal projection shows that the sum of squared limiting coordinates is at most $\|p_0\|_Y^2$; hence the coordinates define a vector $p$ in that closed span. Approximation by finite linear combinations proves weak convergence there, and [F9] represents each functional $x\mapsto\langle x,y\rangle_Y$ restricted to the span, so convergence is weak in $Y$. The limit lies in $K$: by [F2], $K=\bigcap_{z\in X}\{q:\langle q,Az\rangle_Y\le R(z)\}$, an intersection of weakly closed half-spaces. It also attains $\langle f,p\rangle_Y=R(u^\dagger)$, so $p\in P_0$. Weak lower semicontinuity of the norm and the bound force $\|p\|_Y=\|p_0\|_Y$, hence uniqueness gives $p=p_0$. Every subsequence therefore has a further subsequence weakly converging to $p_0$; testing against any fixed $y\in Y$ shows that every scalar subsequence has a further subsequence converging to $\langle p_0,y\rangle_Y$, so $\langle p_n,y\rangle_Y\to\langle p_0,y\rangle_Y$. Thus $p_n\rightharpoonup p_0$. Weak lower semicontinuity and the uniform upper bound then give $\|p_n\|_Y\to\|p_0\|_Y$. The norm identity [F10] yields strong convergence, and boundedness of $A^*$ yields strong convergence of $A^*p_n$. [A1, F1, F2, F8, F9, F10, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

If a marked circle merges with an unmarked one, reducing the output kills $X$ on the marked factor, so $1\otimes1\mapsto1$ and $1\otimes X\mapsto0$. conserved_row.complete_before_row: 1.4 For $0\le u\le1$, interpolate in each normal fibre by $z_u(x)=(1-\chi(u))w_\delta(x)+\chi(u)\delta s(x)$, where $\chi(u)=\sigma(3u-1)$ is the plateau from [F10]. Every $z_u$ has positive pairing with $s$, so it never meets the zero section. Uniformly these vectors have norm $O(\delta)$; a common disk bundle about the compact zero section lies in the tubular domain, so all interpolating graphs lie in that domain when $\delta$ is small. Each graph projects identically to $K$, hence is an embedded circle, and $\Phi$ carries it to an embedded circle disjoint from $K$. With $K$ as the fixed first component this is a smooth two-component link isotopy, stationary near its parameter endpoints, from $K\cup J_0$ to $K\cup\Phi(\delta s)$. The orientation on $J_0$ agrees with the graph orientation because $b_\delta$ preserves orientation. By [F9] the family extends to an ambient isotopy and its linking number is unchanged. The endpoint $\Phi(\delta s)$ is exactly a sufficiently small normalized-chart push-off in [F3]–[F4]. Consequently the self-linking in the statement equals $\operatorname{lk}(K,J_0)$, without identifying the collar level literally with a chart graph of $\delta s$. conserved_row.complete_before_row: 1.3 Use a normalized tubular chart $\Phi$ of $K$ as in [F4] and [F9], and write $\Phi^{-1}(c(p,t))=(b_t(p),v_t(p))$, with $v_t(p)$ in the normal fibre over $b_t(p)$. Compactness permits one small interval of $t$ on which these expressions are defined for every $p$. At $t=0$ they are $(p,0)$, and normalization identifies the vertical derivative with $a(p)s(p)$. The maps $b_t$ are $C^1$-close to the identity. In a smooth oriented circle coordinate their lifts have the form $u+r_t(u)$ with $r_t$ periodic and $\|r_t'\|_\infty<1/2$ for small $t$; thus the lifts are increasing degree-one diffeomorphisms. Hence each $b_t$ is an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism. Reparametrize the level over $x=b_t(p)$, obtaining a smooth normal section $w_t(x)=v_t(b_t^{-1}(x))$. Taylor expansion in finitely many bundle charts gives, uniformly on $K$, $w_t(x)=t a(x)s(x)+O(t^2)$. Because $a$ has positive minimum and $s$ is unit, after decreasing $\delta$ this implies $\langle w_\delta(x),s(x)\rangle>0$ for every $x$. [given, F4, F9, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

conserved_row.complete_before_row: 1.2 The irreducibility assumption applies to $E$: pushing away the deleted-knot end identifies every compact sphere question with that in $Y\setminus K$. A sphere in the interior of $M$ is therefore a sphere disjoint from $F$ in $E$ and bounds a ball in $E$. Since $F$ is connected and disjoint from this sphere, if it entered the ball it would lie wholly in its interior, contradicting $\partial F\subset\partial E$.
